name: Fa’ataupati

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: a patient, precise instructor who counts out loud, demonstrates from the front and the back, repeats every step slowly three times before speeding up, names mistakes kindly and never rushes
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The dance originated in the 19th century as a rhythmic response to a mosquito invasion, turning the act of slapping insects off the skin into a percussive art form.
This is Fa’ataupati. 19th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (K_5MjX8Mj-k)
Title card: Fa’ataupati · Samoa · 19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance was developed in Samoa during the 19th century.
It is historically linked to an invasion of mosquitoes in the Kingdom, where the repetitive motions of slapping insects off the body were transformed into a rhythmic dance.
on_screen: Map: Samoa · Oceania
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance mimics the everyday activity of swatting mosquitoes, representing a cultural adaptation of a historical nuisance into a display of male strength and coordination.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform in a group, maintaining synchronicity while slapping various parts of their bodies including the chest and thighs.
The dance requires strength, stability, and the use of coconut oil on the skin to prevent bruising from the forceful impacts.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (K_5MjX8Mj-k)
Signature moves — MISSING
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: This is the only Samoan dance that requires no external instruments.
The music is created solely through body percussion: slapping the body, clapping hands, and stomping feet.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers typically perform with bare torsos heavily rubbed with coconut oil.
The setting is traditionally communal, though it is now performed on stages globally.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The New Zealand contemporary dance company Black Grace is noted for incorporating Fa’ataupati into their works 'Minoi' and 'Minoi 2'.
The dance is indigenous to Samoans and is classified as the only all-male dance in the culture.

music_brief.purpose: copyright-free soundtrack with the same DNA as the tradition's music — an original creation, not a reproduction
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Fa’ataupati (Samoa). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: the narrator wears the dance's traditional apparel, reconstructed meticulously and respectfully from the sources
wardrobe.from_sources: Dancers typically perform with bare torsos heavily rubbed with coconut oil. The setting is traditionally communal, though it is now performed on stages globally.
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
credits name the tradition and the sources of the reconstruction

visual_brief.costume_notes: Dancers typically perform with bare torsos heavily rubbed with coconut oil. The setting is traditionally communal, though it is now performed on stages globally.
visual_brief.setting_notes: The dance mimics the everyday activity of swatting mosquitoes, representing a cultural adaptation of a historical nuisance into a display of male strength and coordination.
generation_rules: Generated imagery reconstructs costume and setting ONLY from the costume notes above and the licensed images; it is labelled 'reconstruction' on screen.
